newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: Key facts about Moldova before Sunday's election.
newsitem.headline: Key facts about Moldova before Sunday's election.

text.p: Moldova, a former Soviet republic, is holding its first multi-party presidential election on Sunday, and nine candidates are fighting for a mandate to lead the country into the next century.
These are the key facts about Moldova:

POPULATION: 4.33 million including 2.80 million Moldovans (64.4 percent), 600,000 Ukranians (13.8 percent), 562,000 Russians (13 percent), 153,000 Gagauz (3.5 percent), 88,000 Bulgarians (2.0 percent) and 40,000 Jews (1.0 percent).
RELIGION: Over 90 percent of Moldovan citizens belong to the Moldovan Orthodox Church.
LANGUAGE: The official language is known as Moldovan, but is identical to Romanian spoken in neighbouring Romania.
AREA: 33,700 sq km. Landlocked Moldova, previously the south-eastern edge of the former Soviet Union, is flanked by Romanian to the west and Ukraine to the north, east and south.
CAPITAL: Chisinau (population 750,000).
ARMED FORCES: A constitution adopted in July 1994 declared Moldova's "permanent neutrality". Moldova has joined NATO's Partnership for Peace, but does not intend to join NATO.

ECONOMY: Living standards dropped sharply after the mostly agrarian country's economic ties within the old Soviet Union were severed. The country's own lack of energy resources, a 1992 military conflict with pro-Russian separatists in the Dnestr region and severe droughts have worsened the situation.

Officials data say over 40 percent of the population live in poverty, compared to five percent in 1990. The average monthly salary is $40. GDP has fallen 62 percent from its 1992 level, according to official figures and the Economics Ministry puts per capita annual GDP at $350.

Officials expect two percent GDP growth this year after a slide of three percent in 1995 and Moldova has won praise from the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank for its progress in stabilising and restructuring the economy. Loans from these institutions and others total $700 million.

The leu currency, introduced in November 1993, is stable at some 4.60 to the dollar, annual inflation fell to 23.8 percent last year from 105 percent in 1994 and is forecast to slow to 17 percent this year. The 1995 budget deficit was 4.9 percent of GDP from 20 percent in 1992-1993. Private enterprise, encouraged by mass voucher privatisation, makes up 60 percent of GDP.

But foreign investment remains low at around $60 million, partly due to Moldova's uneasy relations with Dnestr separatists and general political instability. Moldova needs big investment programmes to reform its farm sector and large industrial firms, which were once part of the Soviet military-industrial complex.
The country still depends on Russia for energy imports. It owes Russia's gas monopoly Gazprom over $400 million.
HISTORY: Moldovans and Romanians share a common language and cultural heritage. Today's Republic of Moldova was formerly the ancient Romanian principality of Moldova.

Russia won Moldova from Turkey in 1812, ruled it as its province of Bessarabia until 1918. Romania won the territory back in 1918, but it was annexed by Soviet dictator Josef Stalin in 1940 under a secret pact with Nazi Germany. Moldova was one of 15 Soviet republics until the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991.

President Mircea Snegur, who is seeking reelection on Sunday, was elected chairman of parliament in 1989 and appointed president by parliament in 1990. He was the only candidate in Moldova's first presidential election on December 8, 1991.
Snegur, 56, previously one of Moldova's top Communist party members, had been a leading force behind efforts in the 1980s to revive Moldovan historic and cultural values.

But Snegur's brief union with nationalists seeking to reunification with ethnic kin in Romania frightened ethnic minorities. The Gagauz, a 150,000-strong Turkic group in the south of the country, declared themselves independent in August 1990 and in September the Dnestr region in the east of the country broke away. Most of the 700,000 population of the Dnestr region speak Russian or Ukrainian.

Hundreds died when a bloody war between Moldovan security forces and pro-Russian Dnestr rebels broke out in March 1992. The warring factions agreed a ceasefire in August 1992, using Moldovan, Russian and Dnestr forces to keep the peace. Talks about Dnestr's future legal status have stalled over its demand for statehood. Moldova offers broad autonomy.
Some 6,000 Russian soldiers are still based in Dnestr. Gagauzia accepted an autonomy deal with Moldova in 1994.
